1 Introduction

This project explores how population size and growth relate to carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions. It describes the supplied country-level population dataset, projects 2030 population using the specified exponential formula, visualizes population and emissions trends, and compares population with per-capita CO2 emissions.

2 Data preparation and exploratory analysis

The population file contains 234 rows and 17 columns. The CO2 file contains 215 rows and 35 columns before removing its duplicate 2019 column. Population years are available at decadal or selected intervals; CO2 emissions cover each year from 1990 through 2019. The CO2 measure is metric tons per capita, not total national emissions.

The population file has no missing observations, so no imputation or deletion is needed. The CO2 file has 24 missing 2019 emission values; missing CO2 observations are excluded from analyses requiring that year rather than imputed.

2.4 Outlier screening

The table uses the 1.5-IQR rule for selected quantitative variables. The boxplots use a log scale for population, area, and density where that improves readability. Countries with extreme but plausible population, area, or density values are retained; they are not data errors and should not be deleted merely because they are flagged by a boxplot.

kable(outlier_summary, digits = 3,
      caption = "IQR-based outlier counts in selected population variables")

outlier_long <- population |>
  select(country_name, pop_2022, area_km2, density, growth_factor, world_pct) |>
  pivot_longer(-country_name, names_to = "variable", values_to = "value")
ggplot(outlier_long, aes(x = "", y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.45) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Value",
       title = "Distribution and IQR-flagged values") +
  theme_minimal()

3 Population projection to 2030

The supplied Growth Rate is stored as a multiplicative annual factor (for example, 1.01 represents approximately 1% growth). I therefore use the annual decimal rate \(r = \text{Growth Rate} - 1\) and t = 8 years in N[t] = P * exp(r * t), with 2022 population as P. This assumes a constant rate through 2030 and is an illustrative projection, not an official forecast.

top10 |>
  select(country_name, pop_2022, annual_growth_rate, pop_2030) |>
  mutate(across(c(pop_2022, pop_2030), round)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Country", "2022 population", "Annual rate", "Projected 2030"),
        caption = "Projection for the ten most populous countries")

4 Population trends

4.1 Ten most populous countries in 2022

ggplot(top10, aes(x = reorder(country_name, pop_2022), y = pop_2022)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2878B5") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Population",
       title = "Ten most populous countries, 2022") +
  theme_minimal()

4.2 Available population trend observations, 1990-2022

Population observations are available for 1990, 2000, 2010, 2015, 2020, and 2022; the lines connect these observed years and do not imply annual data.

ggplot(top10_trend, aes(x = year, y = population,
                        color = country_name, group = country_name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1990, 2000, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2022)) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Population", color = "Country",
       title = "Population of the 2022 top ten, 1990-2022") +
  theme_minimal()

5 CO2 emissions trend for the top ten

Country codes are used to harmonize country-name variants (for example, different spellings or official names) before joining on canonical country names. CO2 values are per capita. Missing country-year values remain missing and are omitted from the corresponding line segments.

ggplot(top10_co2, aes(x = year, y = co2_per_capita,
                      color = country_name, group = country_name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8, na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "CO2 emissions (metric tons per capita)",
       color = "Country",
       title = "Per-capita CO2 emissions in the 2022 population top ten, 1990-2019") +
  theme_minimal()

6 Correlation analysis

6.1 Population characteristics

The correlations below describe linear association among area, density, annual growth rate, and share of world population. Correlation does not establish causation.

round(correlation_matrix, 3)
##                    area_km2 density annual_growth_rate world_pct
## area_km2              1.000  -0.063             -0.014     0.453
## density              -0.063   1.000             -0.070    -0.028
## annual_growth_rate   -0.014  -0.070              1.000    -0.021
## world_pct             0.453  -0.028             -0.021     1.000
ggplot(correlation_long, aes(variable_x, variable_y, fill = correlation)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", correlation)), size = 4) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#2166AC", mid = "white", high = "#B2182B",
    midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Correlation",
       title = "Population variable correlation heatmap") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1))

6.2 2022 population and 2019 CO2 emissions

The merged analysis includes 191 countries with both 2022 population and non-missing 2019 per-capita emissions. Pearson’s correlation is 0.014 (0.843). The regression below uses log10 population because population is strongly right-skewed; it describes association with per-capita emissions, not total emissions.

ggplot(merged_complete,
       aes(x = pop_2022, y = co2_2019)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.65, color = "#2878B5") +
  geom_smooth(aes(x = pop_2022), method = "lm", se = TRUE,
              formula = y ~ log10(x), color = "#B2182B") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = "2022 population (log scale)",
       y = "2019 CO2 emissions (metric tons per capita)",
       title = "Population size and per-capita CO2 emissions") +
  theme_minimal()

summary(population_co2_model)

7 Comparison by continent

The requested continent comparison sums country-level 2019 per-capita values within each continent. This is an unweighted sum of per-capita indicators; it is not a continent’s total CO2 emissions. A population-weighted estimate or total-emissions dataset would be needed to compare total emissions properly.

kable(continent_totals, digits = 2,
      col.names = c("Continent", "Sum of country per-capita values"),
      caption = "2019 CO2 metric tons per capita summed across available countries")
2019 CO2 metric tons per capita summed across available countries
Continent Sum of country per-capita values
Asia 290.55
Europe 246.67
North America 96.90
Africa 63.73
Oceania 54.78
South America 33.36 
ggplot(continent_totals,
       aes(x = reorder(continent, sum_country_per_capita),
           y = sum_country_per_capita)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#3A923A") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL,
       y = "Sum of country per-capita values (metric tons per capita)",
       title = "2019 per-capita CO2 indicator sums by continent") +
  theme_minimal()

In the requested sum, the first continent is Asia (290.55). The third is North America (96.9) and the last is South America (33.36). These values should be interpreted with the per-capita summation caveat above.

8 Discussion, recommendations, and conclusion

Population grew substantially in several of the most populous countries, but the exponential projection assumes each country’s 2022 growth rate remains constant. Population size alone is not a measure of per-capita emissions, and the country-level association should not be interpreted as a causal effect. The CO2 dataset also contains missing observations and reports emissions per capita, limiting conclusions about total emissions. Future work should use annual population data, document a forecast model and uncertainty, and obtain total emissions or population-weighted per-capita emissions for fair continent-level comparisons.

This analysis applies data inspection, cleaning, visualization, projection, country matching, and correlation/regression methods. The main lesson is that the meaning and units of a variable matter: summing per-capita values does not produce total emissions.
